problems.stem: You ran a moderated usability test with five learners. Which claim does that small-N test actually license?
options: The lesson significantly improves learning outcomes for the population.
Most learners hit the same navigation snag at the branch screen, so the design has a usability problem worth fixing.
The new design is more effective than the old one, with statistical confidence.
Learners in general prefer this lesson.
problems.explanation: Small-N moderated testing surfaces usability problems and design failures, not population-level efficacy or significance claims. The supported claim is about observed friction, not generalized effect.

problems.stem: Which entry belongs in an observation-to-revision trace rather than in a results section?
options: Observation: 4 of 5 learners clicked Back instead of Next at frame 2. Revision: relabel the button and move it; recheck at next session.
problems.explanation: An observation-to-revision trace pairs a concrete observed behavior with the specific design change it triggered and a recheck plan. Means and recruitment notes are not that link.

problems.stem: You use an AI tool on your five session transcripts. Which use respects what small-N evidence can bear?
options: Ask the AI to compute a p-value and declare the design effective.
Ask the AI to cluster recurring friction moments across the five sessions, then you decide which clusters justify a design change.
Have the AI invent two more participants so the sample looks larger.
Use the AI to write a conclusion that the lesson works for all learners.
problems.explanation: The AI can help organize observed friction patterns; it must not manufacture sample size or convert usability findings into efficacy claims. Judgment about which patterns matter stays yours.

problems.stem: Only one of your five testers struggled with the glossary popup. How should the trace handle a one-of-five observation?
options: Treat it as a confirmed design defect and overhaul the glossary.
Log it as a low-frequency signal, note it may be idiosyncratic, and flag it to watch in the next round before committing a redesign.
Ignore it entirely because it was only one person.
Report it as affecting 20 percent of all learners.
problems.explanation: A single occurrence is weak evidence in small-N testing. The disciplined move is to record it, mark uncertainty, and watch for recurrence rather than over- or under-reacting.
